annotation.title_clean: Autonomous Surgical Robots: The Malpractice-Product Liability Boundary
annotation.title_en: Autonomous Surgical Robots: The Malpractice-Product Liability Boundary
annotation.summary_en: Journal article proposing the Autonomy-Control-Risk Attribution (ACRA) framework to decide when harm from autonomous surgical robots falls under medical malpractice, product liability, or concurrent liability, aiming to avoid making surgeons a moral crumple zone. Only abstract and references are available.
key_provisions_or_claims: Malpractice should remain primary where clinicians retain effective control over the relevant clinical risk.
Product-side liability should gain weight where harm stems from hardware, software, algorithms, warnings or autonomous behavior clinicians cannot detect or control.
Where control is distributed, concurrent liability is preferable to forcing a single doctrinal category.
ACRA examines the autonomous function, meaningful human control, risk provenance, informational control and interaction failures.
Surgeons should not become a moral crumple zone for machine-generated decisions.
